abstract: Periodontitis is a bacterially driven inflammatory disease that can lead to tooth mobility and tooth loss. Conventional non-surgical therapy, antibiotics, and surgery may be limited by residual subgingival biofilms, antimicrobial resistance, and variable clinical outcomes. This review synthesizes recent studies of hydrogel-based systems for local periodontal therapy, focusing on stimuli-responsive release mechanisms, cargo-loading approaches, and regenerative outcomes in relevant animal models. Across these studies, hydrogels function as localized delivery matrices that can prolong retention at periodontal defects, regulate therapeutic exposure, and support tissue repair. We further evaluate translational considerations, including degradation behavior, long-termstability, and immunocompatibility. These findings position hydrogels as adaptable platforms for more precise periodontitis management and identify priorities for preclinical optimization before clinical translation.

title: Microbiota-constrained bacterial density limits phage infection in the gut and allows persistence of susceptible cells
abstract: With the rise of antibiotic resistance, bacteriophage-based treatments against bacterial infections have regained momentum. However, phage therapy has so far shown only moderate success in complex environments like the mammalian gut, where phages are particularly promising tools for microbiome engineering and specific elimination of opportunistic pathogens. Here, we use different murine models of intestinal colonization to quantitatively assess the minimal population size of susceptiblecells that is required for phage replication in the gut (replication threshold). We found that the composition of the intestinal microbiota is a key factor shaping phage-bacteria interactions by restricting the carrying capacity of susceptible host cells. We further demonstrate that the replication threshold enables coexistence of susceptible and resistant bacteria in phage-treated mice, with implications for phage-based applications in complex environments like the gut.

title: The plasmid arsenal within: Type IV-A CRISPR-Cas systems in Enterobacteriaceae as modulators of resistance and virulence
abstract: The Enterobacteriaceae family, which includes prominent pathogens such as K. pneumoniae, E. coli, and S. enterica, poses a significant global health threat due to the rapid dissemination of multidrug resistance and virulence determinants. Central to this dissemination are conjugative plasmids, which act as vehicles for horizontal gene transfer. Among the myriad defense systems that interact with these mobile genetic elements, the type IV-A CRISPR-Cas system stands out due to its enigmatic nature and unique plasmid-centric biology. Unlike canonical CRISPR-Cas systems that are chromosomal and target bacteriophages, type IV-A systems are predominantly encoded on large, conjugative plasmids, particularly those bearing IncHI1B/IncFIB replicons. This review synthesizes current evidence on the biology of type IV-A systems within Enterobacteriaceae, elucidating their role as mediators of inter-plasmid competition, their paradoxical association with the spread of antibiotic resistance and virulence genes, and their emerging applications as programmable tools. We explore the mechanistic basis for their function as a natural CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) system, the epidemiological landscape of their distribution, and the dual role they play in both constraining and facilitating the dissemination of clinically relevant traits. Finally, we propose ambitious research avenues, including the development of "plasmid-destroying" probiotics, the use of type IV-A systems as epidemiological biosensors, and the exploration of hypotheses concerning their role in mediating bacterial "altruism" or serving as a "genetic memory" of the plasmid "secretoome."

title: In Vitro Activity of Cefiderocol against Carbapenem-Resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Acinetobacter baumannii and the Cefiderocol Resistance Mechanisms
abstract: Extensively drug-resistant and pandrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria, including Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, pose a major threat due to limited treatment options and high mortality. Rising prevalence of carbapenem resistance has further complicated therapy, necessitating novel antimicrobial agents. Cefiderocol, a siderophore-conjugated cephalosporin, offers a promising therapeutic option against these multidrug-resistant pathogens. To assess the in vitro activity of cefiderocol and key comparators against carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative bacteria from a Malaysian hospital. A total of 448 non-duplicate carbapenem-resistant bacterial strains collected from the University Malaya Medical Centre diagnostic laboratory from year 2018-2021 were included. Broth microdilution was used for susceptibility testing of cefiderocol and other agents relevant to the respective carbapenem-resistant organisms (CROs), in accordance with CLSI guidelines. Susceptibility was interpreted using CLSI breakpoints, with FDA breakpoints applied for tigecycline. Genotypic detection of antimicrobial resistance-associated genes was performed via polymerase chain reaction. Whole genome sequencing was performed on cefiderocol-resistant isolates for genetic characterisation. Cefiderocol demonstrated the highest susceptibility rate for the tested CROs when compared to other antimicrobial agents. More than 90% of the carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae and carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii isolates were susceptible to cefiderocol, whereas 81.2% of carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates were susceptible. Among a total of 22 cefiderocol-resistant isolates, 17 isolates produced NDM-1 and 11 isolates produced PER or VEB ESBL. Cefiderocol remains an effective treatment option for patients infected with CROs. Ongoing surveillance and antibiotic stewardship are essential to monitor the emergence of resistance and preserve the effectiveness of cefiderocol against multidrug-resistant pathogens.

title: Prior ceftriaxone susceptibility and current nonsusceptibility in paired urinary isolates over time: a retrospective longitudinal cohort study
abstract: To quantify how the association between prior ceftriaxone susceptibility and current nonsusceptibility varies across culture intervals and whether it differs by species concordance or recorded antibiotic exposure between cultures. We conducted a retrospective longitudinal cohort study using the 1999-2024 Antibiotic Resistance Microbiology Dataset. Emergency department-associated urine cultures yielding Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, or Proteus mirabilis with direct ceftriaxone susceptibility results were paired with the most recent eligible prior culture obtained more than 14 days earlier. Logistic generalised estimating equations adjusted for age group and anonymised gender code estimated marginal standardised probabilities, risk differences, and risk ratios across eight intervals. The analysis included 4,547 culture pairs from 2,993 patients; 654 current isolates (14.4%) were nonsusceptible. At 15-30 days, the adjusted probability of current nonsusceptibility was 92.3% after a prior nonsusceptible result versus 4.7% after a prior susceptible result; at 31-60 days, probabilities were 88.3% versus 3.8%. Adjusted risk differences were 87.6 and 84.4 percentage points, respectively. Beyond 1095 days, probabilities were 22.1% versus 7.3% (risk difference, 14.8 percentage points; risk ratio, 3.01). The susceptibility-by-interval interaction was significant (P < 0.001). The association was stronger in same-species pairs and differed by recorded antibiotic exposure between cultures (both interaction P < 0.001). Prior ceftriaxone susceptibility provided time-dependent, patient-specific information about current nonsusceptibility. Recent prior nonsusceptibility, particularly with species concordance, was associated with a high probability of current nonsusceptibility, although the association attenuated over time.

title: A case-case-control study of cefovecin use and third-generation cephalosporin-resistant Escherichia coli infections in cats
abstract: To determine if cefovecin administration increased the risk of third-generation cephalosporin (3GC)-resistant Escherichia coli infections in cats. In this retrospective case-case-control study, cases were cats with 3GC-susceptible or 3GC-resistant E coli infections at the Cornell University Hospital for Animals from 2009 to 2023; controls were randomly selected from all feline patients seen during the study period. Exposure data were collected via review of medical records. Direct acyclic graph-driven multivariable regression models of each potential exposure were built for each case-control grouping. 36 susceptible cases (3% cefovecin treated), 14 resistant cases (21% cefovecin treated), and 72 controls (6% cefovecin treated) were identified. Resistant cases had a higher proportion of cefovecin use (21%) than susceptible cases (3%) and controls (6%), but case numbers were too low to evaluate whether cefovecin use was associated with either infection type. Most of the cats that received cefovecin (75%) were underdosed. The overall frequency of cefovecin administration was low (7%) compared to previous studies. Cefovecin use was less frequent than previously reported, resulting in too few cases to determine whether cefovecin use is associated with 3GC-resistant E coli infections in cats. The sample size was too small to evaluate association between cefovecin and 3CG resistance. Based on prudent antimicrobial stewardship, veterinarians should limit cefovecin use to cases where oral antimicrobial treatment is impossible and, ideally, its use is supported by antimicrobial susceptibility testing to avoid selecting for antimicrobial resistance in treated cats. When using cefovecin, veterinarians should ensure they are administering the label-recommended 8-mg/kg dose.

title: Current and emerging threats to honey bee health: a One Health perspective on antibiotic pollution
abstract: Pollinators play a critical role in global food production and ecosystem health, yet high losses of essential honey bee colonies have been reported worldwide. Climate change, habitat loss, parasites, pesticides, and poor nutrition are established pollinator threats, whereas environmental antibiotic pollution remains poorly understood. Antibiotic exposure may independently affect bees or interact with these stressors, potentially compounding adverse health effects. Synthetic antibiotic residues and resistance genes enter the environment through the fertilization of soils with antibiotic-containing animal manure, animal wastewater discharge, and airborne antibiotic contamination landing directly on flowers and crops. While the effects of direct antibiotic exposure on honey bees have been studied, the consequences of indirect environmental exposure remain largely unknown. Foraging bees may encounter antibiotic contaminants in the environment, potentially disrupting their gut microbiome, altering behavior and physiology, and increasing susceptibility to pathogens. Contamination of honey bees and their products with antibiotics serve not only as indicators of environmental antibiotic resistance but also as a practical One Health model linking human, animal, and environmental health. Studying honey bee responses to agricultural contaminants provides insight into how antibiotic resistance and environmental stressors can move across ecosystems, affecting both pollinators and the broader public. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the multifactor threats to honey bees and their mitigation strategies, emphasizing the influence of animal production and antibiotic pollution on honey bee health. We highlight knowledge gaps in understanding the transfer of antibiotic resistance from agricultural environments to honey bees to enhance pollinator health and promote long-term ecological resilience.

title: Plasmid-mediated dissemination of antimicrobial resistance among multidrug-resistant bacteria isolated from food-contact surfaces in university cafeterias
abstract: Food-contact surfaces may facilitate the spread of antimicrobial-resistant bacteria in food-service settings. We examined 42 samples (spoons, plates, forks, drinking cups, chopping boards, and washing water; six per cafeteria) from seven university cafeterias in Peshawar, Pakistan. Twenty-seven samples (64.3%) yielded growth: Escherichia coli (8; 29.6%), Staphylococcus aureus (6; 22.2%), Klebsiella pneumoniae (5; 18.5%), Enterobacter cloacae (5; 18.5%), and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (3; 11.1%), identified by biochemical tests and 16 S rRNA sequencing. Chopping boards and washing water were most frequently contaminated. Resistance to β-lactams was common, whereas meropenem remained active against most isolates. Sixteen isolates (59.3%) were multidrug-resistant (MDR) and three (11.1%) were extensively drug-resistant. Among MDR isolates, blaTEM (68.75%) and blaCTX-M (62.5%) were the most frequent of 12 genes screened by PCR, followed by tetA, blaSHV, blaOXA, aac(6')-Ib, qnrA, qnrB, sul1, tetM, blaNDM, and mecA. Eleven of 13 MDR Gram-negative isolates carried plasmids, and seven of these 11 transferred β-lactam resistance to E. coli J53 in filter-mating assays. These findings indicate that cafeteria food-contact surfaces can harbor MDR bacteria with potentially transferable resistance genes, supporting improved sanitation and routine surveillance.

title: Effect of continuous application of pig manure on soil antibiotic resistance genes
abstract: The large-scale application of livestock and poultry manure in protected agriculture is common; however, research on the spread of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) from this practice remains limited. Herein, 16 S and metagenomic sequencing methods were used to investigate the effects of eight consecutive years of pig manure application on tetracycline (TC) antibiotics in protected soil and to evaluate the ecological consequences. In addition, the characteristics of soil ARGs and bacterial diversity were explored, and the potential hosts of ARGs in protected soil and the influence of environmental factors on these potential hosts and ARGs were preliminarily investigated. After 8 years of applying composted pig manure, the total tetracycline residues in the protected soil was as follows: commercial organic fertilizer soil > pig manure soil > rapeseed cake fertilizer soil. Soil enzymes indirectly affect ARG abundance by influencing the microbial community structure. g__unclassified_p__Acidobacteria and g__unclassified_c__Actinomycetia may be the two most important ARG hosts, with a highly significant positive correlation with 32 ARG subtypes. Total nitrogen (TN) and soil organic matter (SOM) significantly promoted the abundance of these two important potential hosts. Nocardioides, g__unclassified_o__Solirubrobacterales, Actinoplanes, and Methyloceanibacter are potential hosts for intI1. TC, Soil urease(S-UE), Soil acid phosphatase(ACP), Soil β-glucosidase(S-β-GC), TN, total phosphorus (TP), and SOM significantly promoted the abundance of potential intI1 hosts. Soil environmental factors collectively accounted for 72.27% of ARG variation, making them the most important factor affecting ARGs. Our research will support manure management in protected agriculture to reduce ARG spread.

title: Repurposing proton pump inhibitors to restore ceftriaxone activity against multidrug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae: phenotypic, molecular, and in silico evidence
abstract: Klebsiella pneumoniae has emerged as one of the most clinically significant multidrug-resistant (MDR) pathogens, with multidrug efflux systems playing a pivotal role in antibiotic resistance and therapeutic failure. This study investigated the contribution of the efflux-associated genes kpnE, kmrA, and kdeA to ceftriaxone resistance and evaluated proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) as efflux pump-targeting adjuvants. Fifty clinical K. pneumoniae isolates were characterized by antimicrobial susceptibility testing, MDR/XDR classification, phenotypic efflux activity assays, molecular detection of efflux-associated genes, kpnE sequencing, quantitative real-time PCR, molecular docking, and ceftriaxone minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) determination in the presence and absence of omeprazole and lansoprazole. MDR and XDR phenotypes were identified in 70% and 18% of isolates, respectively, whereas active efflux was detected in 14% of isolates and was significantly associated with increasing resistance severity. Sequence analysis demonstrated marked conservation of kpnE, with a single D → G amino acid substitution identified in one isolate. Despite this conservation, gene expression analysis revealed substantial isolate-dependent transcriptional responses that were not directly correlated with phenotypic efflux activity, suggesting that transporter efficiency is governed by complex interactions between transcriptional regulation, structural adaptation, and protein functionality rather than gene expression alone. Molecular docking demonstrated favorable binding of both PPIs to KpnE, KmrA, and KdeA, supporting their potential to interfere with efflux-mediated drug extrusion. Consistent with these predictions, combination assays markedly potentiated ceftriaxone activity, reducing MIC values by up to 16,516-fold and restoring ceftriaxone susceptibility in all seven tested efflux-active ceftriaxone-resistant isolates, with omeprazole producing the greatest synergistic effect. Collectively, these findings provide new mechanistic insight into the role of SMR-associated efflux systems in K. pneumoniae antimicrobial resistance and identify proton pump inhibitors, particularly omeprazole, as potential antibiotic adjuvants for restoring β-lactam efficacy against MDR and XDR K. pneumoniae. Further functional and in vivo studies are warranted to determine whether these in vitro findings can be translated into clinically relevant therapeutic applications.

title: Epidemiological and antimicrobial susceptibility patterns of Staphylococcus aureus isolated from the nasal cavity of healthcare personnel at a public hospital in Northeastern Brazil: a cross-sectional survey
abstract: Nasal colonization by Staphylococcus aureus among healthcare professionals represents a potential risk for the spread of resistant strains in hospital settings. Thus, this cross-sectional study aimed to determine the prevalence of nasal colonization by S. aureus and to characterize the antimicrobial resistance profile of the isolated strains from professionals working in a public hospital in Caxias, Maranhão, Brazil. This study was carried out from December 2024 to February 2025. A total of 132 professionals working in a public hospital in the state of Maranhão were included. Among the participants, 36 (27.27%) were colonized by S. aureus, and 6 isolates (16.66%) were identified as methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA). High resistance rates were observed to penicillin G and ampicillin (94.4%), as well as to the macrolides erythromycin (83.3%) and azithromycin (77.8%). Resistance to tetracycline was detected in 11.1% of the isolates, with 22.2% showing intermediate susceptibility. All isolates were susceptible to clindamycin, chloramphenicol, and rifampicin. Regarding risk factors, working in two healthcare locations compared to one remained significantly associated with nasal colonization after adjustment (OR = 3.15-3.50; p < 0.05), whereas longer professional experience was identified as a protective factor (OR ranging from 0.11 to 0.17; p < 0.05). These findings demonstrate the circulation of multidrug-resistant S. aureus strains among healthcare professionals and highlight the importance of active surveillance, rational antimicrobial use, and strengthened infection control strategies to reduce the spread of resistant pathogens in hospital environments.

title: Dual-mode biosensing featuring fluorescence and electrochemiluminescence for regional resolution of single-nucleotide variants
abstract: Single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) are a critical molecular basis for antibiotic resistance in pathogenic bacteria. However, precise detection of mutant targets remains challenging because they may exist at low abundance and often coexist with wild-type sequences in complex biological matrices. Herein, we report a target-triggered strand displacement reaction that releases two functional DNA strands: one activates the trans-cleavage activity of CRISPR/Cas12a to generate a fluorescent signal, while the other competitively displaces cadmium sulfide quantum dots pre-modified on a gold electrode surface, decreasing the electrochemiluminescence (ECL) signal. The two functional strands hybridize to distinct regions of the probe, enabling the two signaling channels to respond differentially to single-base mismatches at different locations. Taking the response to wild-type targets as a reference, synchronized changes in both signals reflect target concentration. A significant decrease in the fluorescence signal alone, with the ECL signal unchanged, indicates that the mismatch occurs within the fluorescence recognition region, whereupon the unaffected ECL channel may serve for quantification. Conversely, when the ECL signal decreases while the fluorescence signal remains stable, the fluorescence channel may serve for quantification. This design enables a single probe to discriminate between wild-type and mutant targets based on the differential responses of the two signaling channels. Our strategy thus provides a new avenue for single-base nucleic acid detection.

title: Carbapenemase-Producing Carbapenem-Resistant Enterobacterales Among Children in the United States, 2019-2024
abstract: The current epidemiology of carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) among pediatric patients in the United States is poorly described. We assessed trends in pediatric CRE and carbapenemase-producing-CRE (CP-CRE) incidence in the U.S. and characterized recent pediatric CP-CRE cases. We analyzed CRE clinical isolates from patients <18 years submitted to CDC's Antimicrobial Resistance Laboratory Network from January 2019 through December 2024. Annual unadjusted incidence rates for CRE and CP-CRE were estimated overall and by age group for a national convenience sample and an open cohort of 29 states with required CRE isolate submission. Trends were assessed using Poisson regression. For pediatric patients with incident CP-CRE identified from January 2023 through March 2024, medical chart reviews were performed. From 2019-2024, the estimated national pediatric CRE and CP-CRE incidence increased 51% (IRR:1.51; 95% CI:1.22, 1.88) and 92% (IRR:1.92; 95% CI:1.25, 2.99), respectively; increases were similar in the open cohort. Infants had the highest incidence rates. Overall, NDM-CRE incidence increased (IRR: 4.24; 95% CI: 2.07, 9.16), surpassing KPC-CRE as the most prominent carbapenemase. Chart reviews were completed for 109 of 129 pediatric patients with CP-CRE; 14% were in patients without healthcare risk factors. Among patients with healthcare risk factors, 75% had an underlying medical condition; the most common underlying condition among infants and toddlers was cardiovascular disease (64%) and among older children was neurocognitive conditions (49%) and malignancies (41%). Common exposures across all age groups included intensive care unit hospitalization (40%) and healthcare outside the United States (37%). Pediatric CP-CRE incidence is increasing, driven by NDM-CRE for which there are few treatment options. Most cases occurred among children with serious underlying conditions receiving high-acuity care. Prevention opportunities may include admission screening for patients with prior healthcare exposure outside the United States and strengthening infection prevention practices.

title: Essential oils for acute cystitis: a real-world experience in primary care settings
abstract: Acute cystitis is a significant public health challenge, with escalating antimicrobial: resistance threatening conventional antibiotic therapy. Essential oils (EOs) containing bioactive compounds such as carvacrol and cinnamaldehyde, offer multi-target antimicrobial mechanisms that may provide effective alternatives while supporting antimicrobial stewardship efforts. This real-world observational study compared the clinical efficacy of an EO-based formulation with that of standard antibiotic therapy in women with acute cystitis. 68 patients participated: Groups A (N.=24), treated with fosfomycin trometamol 3 g single-dose; Group B (N.=21) received the EO combination (OLEOBIOTICSalud urinaria manufactured by Pranarom International S.A.) at the standard dose (1 capsule 3 times daily for 5 days); Group C (N.=23) received the double dosage. OLEOBIOTICSalud urinaria is a food supplement manufactured by Pranarom International S.A. and formulated with EOs of oregano (Origanum vulgare) 10 mg, Chinese cinnamon (Cinnamomum cassia) 30 mg, lemon (Citrus limon) 5 mg, lemongrass (Cymbopogon citratus) 40 mg, thyme (Thymus vulgaris, thymol chemotype) 20 mg, savory (Satureja montana) 20 mg, cloves (Caryophyllus aromaticus) 10 mg, and fennel (Foeniculum vulgare) 15 mg. Primary outcomes was urinary dipstick test negativization. Secondary outcomes assessed symptom severity, patient satisfaction, antibiotic avoidance, and safety profile. Urinary dipstick negativization rates were comparable across groups: Group A 83.3%, Group B 90.5%, and Group C 78.3% (P>0.05). All groups showed a significant improvement in urinary frequency (P<0.001), with patients urinating ≤4 times daily increasing from baseline to post-treatment: Group A from 25.0% to 70.8%, Group B from 19.0% to 85.7%, and Group C from 21.7% to 69.6%. Antibiotic prescription was avoided in 66.7-78.3% of cases. Patient satisfaction was high across all groups, with 71.4% to 100% willing to use the treatment again. Only one adverse event (self-limiting diarrhea) was reported, with no recurrences during follow-up. EO-based formulations demonstrated clinically significant efficacy in the managing of acute cystitis, with high dipstick negativization rates, substantial symptom relief, and excellent safety profile. The multi-target antimicrobial mechanisms of key components offer theoretical advantages for reducing the development of resistance. These findings may support integrating natural treatments into clinical algorithms for uncomplicated cystitis as part of comprehensive antimicrobial stewardship strategies. Nevertheless, randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm these real-world observations.

title: Estimating Marginal Effects on Survival Outcomes for Clinical Interpretations and Decision Making
abstract: The Cox regression model is the most widely used method in survival analysis, but the hazard ratio has limited clinical interpretability. Survival or cumulative incidence curves are often used to illustrate treatment effects, yet there is no consensus on the most appropriate methods for generating these curves, particularly in the presence of confounding and competing risks. We reviewed original research articles published in a general medical journal in 2025, identified limitations in common practices, and describe a marginal effects framework to generate adjusted cumulative incidence curves that are coherent with the analysis model, anchored in absolute risk estimates, and adaptable to competing risks and clustered data. The framework targets the population-average difference in cumulative incidence between exposure groups, under the assumptions of no unmeasured confounding, positivity, and non-informative censoring. As a demonstration, we applied the framework to real-world data from Yek et al. (2025) and showed that it produced clinically interpretable estimates of hospital-acquired antimicrobial resistance risk that a single hazard ratio could not convey. To facilitate implementation, we describe each analytic step in detail, discuss available software, and share an R program with core routines written in C for computational efficiency.

title: Porcine Oral Fluid as a Diagnostic Matrix for Tulathromycin and Enrofloxacin Residue Surveillance
abstract: Antibiotic analysis is an important aspect of pig farming due to residues in tissues and the spread of antimicrobial resistance. In vivo control of antimicrobials is particularly significant, especially for the most critical and widely administered drugs. Thus, the aim of this study was to investigate the concentrations of tulathromycin and enrofloxacin in oral fluid after pig treatment. The analysis was performed by an ultrahigh-performance liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (UHPLC-MS/MS) method. Both drugs were detected for 31 days after the end of the treatment. On the last day of sampling, the concentration of tulathromycin was 19.7 μg/L and that of enrofloxacin was 26.4 μg/L. Tulathromycin reached its peak concentration (2180 μg/L) on day 2, while the highest concentration of enrofloxacin (1250 μg/L) was recorded on day 1 postadministration. The obtained results confirm the feasibility of detecting the two tested compounds in oral fluid, demonstrating a new approach for antemortem antibiotic control in pigs.

title: Antibiotic class shapes O-antigen-dependent phage outcomes in a clinical Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolate
abstract: is a high-priority opportunistic pathogen characterized by significant genetic plasticity and increasing multidrug resistance. Although phage-antibiotic combinations are increasingly explored to combat antimicrobial resistance, whether these interactions are synergistic or antagonistic and how different antibiotic classes influence phage replication and the subsequent development of resistance remain unclear. In this study, we examined combinations of the O-antigen-dependent phage phipa10 with amikacin (AMK), levofloxacin (LEV), or meropenem (MEM) againstZS-PA-35. At 24 h, the combinations showed antibiotic-dependent patterns of bacterial growth suppression. High concentrations of amikacin and meropenem reduced the extracellular yield of infectious phipa10. The highest tested levofloxacin concentration also reduced the recovered phage yield. Whole-genome sequencing of phage-resistant mutants showed that meropenem treatment drove large chromosomal deletions encompassingand, resulting in a characteristic brown pigmentation phenotype. LEV-selected isolates carried smaller deletions involving, whereas AMK-selected isolates shared asubstitution. In ainfection model, phipa10-antibiotic combinations improved host survival relative to either treatment alone, although the magnitude of the benefit varied across antibiotic classes. The meropenem combination yielded the highest observed survival proportion despite reduced phage yield. These results show that bacterial suppression, infectious phage yield, and resistance outcomes can diverge among the three tested antibiotic partners.IMPORTANCEPhage-antibiotic combinations may affect bacterial suppression, phage yield, and resistance-associated phenotypes differently. We compared three antibiotic partners in a single-phage system. The observed growth, genetic, and larval survival outcomes varied across the tested treatments. Reduced phage yield did not preclude improved survival in the infection model. These observations support evaluating multiple outcomes when assessing a phage-antibiotic combination. Their broader relevance requires validation with additional isolates, phages, and antibiotics.

title: Stability of therapeutic bacteriophages in clinically approved crystalloid infusion solutions
abstract: The growing burden of antimicrobial resistance underscores the need for effective alternatives to conventional antibiotics, with bacteriophage therapy representing a promising approach. However, insufficient product stability during storage and administration may reduce the delivered dose and confound assessments of clinical efficacy. Clinically approved crystalloid infusion solutions could facilitate phage preparation and administration, but their suitability for phage storage remains poorly characterized. The stability of four virulent bacteriophages targetingorwas evaluated in sodium chloride 0.45%, sodium chloride 0.9%, Ringer's lactate, Ringer's acetate, and saline magnesium (SM) buffer. Phage preparations containing 10⁹ plaque-forming units per mL were stored at 4°C, -20°C, or -80°C, with or without 10% glycerol, for up to 6 months. Phage infectivity was highly dependent on the phage, solution, and storage temperature. Buffered solutions generally preserved infectivity better than saline, particularly under frozen conditions. Glycerol improved stability during freezing, although the magnitude of this effect varied among phages and was most apparent in saline solutions. Storage at -80°C with glycerol provided the most consistent preservation across all four phages, with titers remaining close to baseline. Ringer's solutions supported high stability at -80°C also without glycerol. By contrast, storage at 4°C resulted in greater variability and reduced stability for several phages. These findings demonstrate that clinically approved crystalloid solutions can serve as vehicles for both phage storage and administration and suggest a need for phage-specific stability testing. Reliable bacteriophage therapy requires formulations that preserve phage activity during storage and clinical administration. Yet, standardized approaches to phage formulation and storage remain lacking, and many clinical applications still rely on empirical practices rather than evidence-based pharmaceutical principles. This study addresses an important translational barrier by examining the stability of therapeutically relevant phages targetingandin crystalloid solutions routinely used for intravenous administration. Comparison of distinct phages across different formulations, temperatures, and storage durations demonstrates that stability depends strongly on the individual phage and storage conditions. These findings expand the limited evidence on phage stability in clinically applicable formulations and reinforce the rationale for individual phage stability testing during product development to ensure the delivery of an active and consistent therapeutic dose.

title: Isolation, Identification, and Whole Genome Sequencing Analysis of Common Foodborne Bacteria from Fresh Fruits, Vegetables, and Their Ready-to-Eat Products in Shijiazhuang, China
abstract: With evolving lifestyles, consumer demand for fresh fruits and vegetables has increased. However, these products are susceptible to contamination by foodborne bacteria from farm to table. To investigate the contamination status of foodborne bacteria in commercially available fresh fruits, vegetables, and their ready-to-eat (RTE) products in Shijiazhuang City, a total of 406 samples were collected from 2024 to 2025.(),(), diarrheagenic(diarrheagenic), andwere identified and analyzed for genomic characteristics using traditional biochemical tests and whole genome sequencing (WGS). The results showed that the detection rate ofwas 4.68% (19/406), of which 5 isolates were identified as methicillin-resistant(MRSA), accounting for 1.23% (5/406). The detection rate ofwas 8.37% (34/406), and the detection rate of diarrheagenicwas 0.25% (1/406). Nowas detected. Genomic characterization revealed thatstrains were predominantly ST59 and ST22, with the MRSA strains primarily identified as ST59-SCCmec-IVa (2B)-t437. A total of 20 enterotoxin genes were detected, with 94.74% (18/19) of the strains carrying at least one enterotoxin gene. Thegene was the most prevalent (52.63%, 10/19), and thegene, which can cause toxic shock syndrome, was detected in 2 strains.isolates were divided into 30 STs, exhibiting high genetic diversity. All toxin types were classified as type A. Thegene showed the highest carriage rate of resistance genes (94.12%, 32/34), and the main resistance profile was+(55.88%, 19/34). title: Viral potential to modulate antibiotic resistance gene succession through host interactions during food waste composting
abstract: Composting can mitigate antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) risks, yet viral contributions to their dynamics remain unclear. Using time-series metagenomics, we investigated viral roles in ARG succession during composting of two food waste types. In both composts, ARGs followed an enrichment-decline-rebound trajectory accompanied by substrate-specific ARG-host turnover. Particularly, the maturation rebound involved the re-enrichment of high-risk ARGs, including tet(L) and lnu(G). Procrustes analysis showed significant associations of viral communities with bacterial and ARG profiles. Meanwhile, virus-host networks were organized predominantly around Firmicutes, with both temperate and lytic viral abundances correlated with ARG-host dynamics during the heating-to-thermophilic transition. Viral auxiliary metabolic genes (AMGs), annotated for central carbon metabolism, nutrient acquisition, and stress responses, may aid environmental adaptation in key ARG hosts, including Bacillus spp. Although mobile genetic elements (MGEs) provided important genetic contexts for ARG mobility, only four putative virus-mediated ARG horizontal transfer records were detected. Structural equation modelling suggested potential viral involvement through host interactions, while highlighting the importance of ARG hosts and MGEs in resistome succession. Further viral perturbation experiments are needed to clarify causal contributions in future. Overall, this study provides new insights into viral roles in resistome succession, informing resistance risk management during composting.

title: Values and trade-offs in responsible antibiotic behaviour and sustainable access: protocol for a comparative mixed-methods empirical ethics study in Sweden, Italy, and Bulgaria
abstract: Antibiotic resistance arises through biological evolution but is also shaped by behavioural, sociocultural, and institutional factors. Promoting responsible antibiotic behaviour requires understanding how members of the public and relevant stakeholders perceive antibiotic use, stewardship, access, and responsibility, and the values and trade-offs that shape their decisions. This study aims to investigate these factors across three national contexts and to develop context-sensitive recommendations and a methodological framework for future research. This protocol describes an ongoing comparative mixed-methods empirical ethics study conducted in Sweden, Italy, and Bulgaria from May 2025 to April 2028. The study comprises three connected components: semi-structured online interviews with 16-20 participants from four stakeholder groups in each country; a general-population survey incorporating a discrete choice experiment, with a minimum of 350 respondents per country; and iterative normative analysis using reflective equilibrium. The 3D Value Framework informs the interviews, which examine stakeholders' reasoning about sustainable antibiotic access, stewardship, responsibility, and preparedness. Interview findings, relevant literature, and previous research will inform the survey attributes and scenarios. The survey will examine public preferences and trade-offs concerning antibiotic treatment, responsible behaviour, and sustainable access, alongside antibiotic knowledge, trust, prosociality, biospherism, gender-related perspectives, social norms, and values. The empirical findings will be interpreted in relation to ethical theories of justice and personal and collective responsibility. A One Health perspective informs the overall study. By bringing stakeholder reasoning and public preferences into dialogue with normative analysis, the study will examine how responsibility for preserving antibiotic effectiveness and sustainable access should be understood and distributed between individuals and institutional actors. It will also address the ethical implications of trade-offs between present and future access and the distribution of associated benefits and burdens. This empirical ethics approach is expected to support a context-sensitive account of justice and responsibility and to inform ethically justified antibiotic stewardship, policy, and communication. Not applicable.

title: A sequence-informed hybrid framework for predicting antibiotic minimum inhibitory concentrations in previously unseen Escherichia coli pathogens
abstract: When an Escherichia coli pathogen is newly encountered, antimicrobial susceptibility information may be incomplete or unavailable. We investigated whether minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) could be predicted for previously unseen pathogens by jointly using pathogen genomic sequence information, antibiotic characteristics, and observed pathogen-antibiotic MIC patterns. The predictive value of integrating pathogen genomic information, antibiotic characteristics, and observed pathogen-antibiotic MIC patterns within a hybrid collaborative-filtering framework for previously unseen E. coli pathogens remains unclear. To develop and evaluate Model C for predicting MIC values in previously unseen, genomically characterised E. coli pathogens. The study used 9377 E. coli pathogens, 26 antibiotics, and 51,554 exact MIC measurements among 243,802 possible pathogen-antibiotic combinations. Model C combined observed MIC patterns, genomic features related to antimicrobial resistance (AMR), nucleotide-sequence comparisons across 265 AMR-related loci, and antibiotic characteristics. Five-fold pathogen-out validation excluded all MIC measurements from each test pathogen from training and model selection. The common validation cohort contained 9058 pathogens and 50,460 observed MIC values; Models 3B and 3 were evaluated as comparators. In pathogen-out validation of the 50,460 observed MIC values, Model C achieved a mean absolute error of 0.5931 log₂ MIC units, root mean squared error of 0.8477, and Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.9055. Model C performed best overall. A final model fitted to all 50,460 observed MICs predicted the remaining 185,048 unmeasured MICs. Model C estimated MIC values for previously unseen E. coli pathogens using genomic, antibiotic, and observed interaction information. Independent external validation is required. Predictions may help prioritise confirmatory testing but should not replace antimicrobial susceptibility testing or be used alone to guide treatment.

title: Emissions of quaternary ammonium compounds and pharmaceuticals from wastewater treatment plants under different operational conditions
abstract: The use of both quaternary ammonium compounds (QACs)-biocides increasingly consumed after the outbreak of covid-19-and pharmaceuticals causes concerns about adverse effects on aquatic organisms and links to antimicrobial resistance. Though they largely enter wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs), there exists a gap in knowledge of the effects of solids retention time (SRT) and hydraulic retention time (HRT) on their removal in the activated sludge process. We monitored 14 QACs, another disinfectant, and 13 pharmaceuticals in treated effluents of 14 activated sludge WWTPs with wide ranges of SRT (5-48 days) and HRT (7-70 h), within an administrative district over a year. The total mean concentrations of all compounds ranged from 2.4 to 15 μg/L among the WWTP effluents, to which 14 labile compounds (11 QACs and 3 drugs) contributed 6% to 76%. Their contributions were higher in WWTPs with shorter SRTs and HRTs. Relative standard deviations (RSDs) of effluent concentrations of labile compounds were mostly >50% among seasons and >100% among the WWTPs, largely exceeding those in raw sewage. The higher the WWTP removal rate of a compound was, the larger the effluent RSD was among the WWTPs and seasons. Per-capita mass outflows of most compounds other than persistent drugs were negatively correlated with SRTs or HRTs among the WWTPs, indicating that they were key factors affecting their removal and emission. Interpretation of these associations should consider the limited number of WWTPs and the availability of operational data. Our findings will be useful in managing QACs and pharmaceuticals.

title: Isolation, characterization, and therapeutic potential of a novel phage vB_KpiP_JZBo1 infecting Klebsiella pneumoniae
abstract: Klebsiella pneumoniae (K. pneumoniae) is an important opportunistic pathogenic bacterium that is often characterized by a multidrug-resistant phenotype, which can lead to the failure of antibiotic treatments. The emergence of multidrug-resistant K. pneumoniae, including carbapenem-resistant K. pneumoniae (CRKP), poses a significant threat to public health security. Bacteriophages, which are viruses capable of lysing bacteria, represent a promising alternative for treating infections caused by highly virulent K. pneumoniae and other antibiotic-resistant pathogens. In this study, we used K. pneumoniae 32b as the host bacterium and isolated the bacteriophage vB_KpiP_JZBo1. The optimal MOI of this bacteriophage is 0.01. And phage exhibited high activity across a wide range of temperatures (20°C - 50°C) and pH (4 - 11) following 1 h of incubation. Whole genome analysis revealed that the bacteriophage was a double-stranded DNA virus, encoding a total of 91 open reading frames (ORFs). Notably, genetic evolutionary analysis and BLASTN results indicated that phage vB_KpiP_JZBo1 shares the closest evolutionary relationship with K. pneumoniae phage KP8. However, genome-wide comparison revealed that they only exhibit 88% coverage and 93.03% nucleotide homology. This suggests that phage vB_KpiP_JZBo1 may be a novel species of phage. No genes associated with antibiotic resistance, virulence factors, and tRNA were found in the phage genome, and it belongs to Kaypoctavirus genus of the Schitoviridae family. Additionally, higher phage doses resulted in greater inhibitory and bactericidal effects against K. pneumoniae in LB medium. In model of G. mellonella, bacteriophage vB_KpiP_JZBo1 can effectively eliminate the infection of K. pneumoniae 32b and increase the survival rate of G. mellonella. These findings suggest that the bacteriophage vB_KpiP_JZBo1 has potential for the treatment and prevention of K. pneumoniae, and they also provide a theoretical basis for clinical applications.

title: Comparative effects and mechanisms of microbial inoculants and enzyme preparations on vermicomposting performance and antibiotic resistance reduction
abstract: Antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in livestock manure pose risks to soil ecosystems and human health, yet their attenuation during vermicomposting remains incomplete even with earthworm activity. This study systematically evaluated whether two functional additive types, namely microbial inoculants and enzyme preparations, could enhance vermicompost conversion efficiency, compost quality, and ARG attenuation in cattle manure vermicomposting. Our results showed that most additives altered physicochemical properties and improved compost maturity, with the commercial compound microbial inoculant KM (trade name) achieving a germination index above 140%. Notably, acid protease treatment (VES) achieved a 27.5-percentage-point greater reduction in combined ARGs and integron-marker abundance than the unamended vermicomposting control (58.0% vs. 30.5%), indicating its potential for enhanced reduction of resistance-related abundance. Mechanistically, microbial inoculants (e.g., KM) effectively weakened ARG-integron marker-microbial co-occurrence associations through ecological network restructuring, whereas enzyme preparations (represented by acid protease) induced coordinated shifts in physicochemical properties and microbial community structure, which were associated with reduced ARG abundance. Additionally, spatial niche differentiation along the earthworm gut was associated with resistance-class-specific ARG distribution patterns. These findings indicate that microbial inoculants and enzyme preparations act through distinct ecological pathways in attenuating antibiotic resistance, providing a mechanistic basis for targeted additive selection in sustainable livestock manure valorization.

title: Could the next pandemic be fungal and could we respond effectively? From plausible pathways to operational preparedness
abstract: Fungal diseases cause substantial morbidity and mortality worldwide, yet they have been persistently neglected in pandemic preparedness plans, largely because no sustained human-to-human fungal pandemic has been documented to date. However, multidisciplinary evidence challenges the assumption that fungi are irrelevant to pandemic risk. Wildlife fungal pandemics show that mycoses can emerge on a global scale with catastrophic and irreversible consequences. Moreover, climate change is narrowing the mammalian thermal barrier against fungi, favouring heat-tolerant species, reshaping their global distribution, and thus facilitating zoonotic spillover. Rising human susceptibility-driven by ageing populations, immunomodulatory therapies, and increasingly complex health care-is intersecting with a substantial therapeutic gap, characterised by the absence of licensed vaccines, a limited range of antifungal agents, and increasing antimicrobial resistance. In this Personal View, we move beyond a synthesis of evidence to propose an operational framework for fungal pandemic preparedness, outlining plausible routes to pandemic-scale impact and the surveillance, diagnostic, therapeutic, One Health, and outbreak-response capacities needed to detect and contain emerging fungal threats before they become unmanageable.

title: Multi-Parameter In Vitro and Genomic Characterization of Bovine-Derived Bacteria with Probiotic Potential
abstract: Raw milk and bovine feces represent important sources of microorganisms with probiotic potential. This study aimed to identify potential probiotic candidates from bovine-derived samples and to comprehensively characterize their functional and safety-related features by integrating multi-parameter in vitro evaluation with whole-genome analysis. Acid-producing bacteria were isolated from 12 raw milk and 15 bovine fecal samples using bromocresol green agar. Following PCR-based exclusion of Escherichia coli and RAPD-PCR dereplication, the isolates were evaluated for acid and bile tolerance, survival under simulated gastrointestinal conditions, and autoaggregation, leading to the selection of five candidate strains: Lactiplantibacillus plantarum MX13, Lacticaseibacillus paracasei MX165, Enterococcus faecalis MX179, Enterococcus faecium MX125, and Enterococcus durans FX198. Further in vitro characterization revealed marked strain-specific differences in gastrointestinal stress tolerance, autoaggregation, cell-surface hydrophobicity, and antibacterial activity, with the two lactobacilli displaying broader antibacterial spectra than the Enterococcus strains. Multivariate analysis further revealed distinct overall phenotypic profiles among the candidates, with MX13 exhibiting a relatively balanced functional profile across the traits evaluated. Whole-genome analysis revealed clear differences between MX13 and MX125 in antimicrobial resistance-associated, putative virulence-associated, and other functional genomic features, providing additional information for candidate prioritization. Overall, this study identified and characterized five bovine-derived potential probiotic candidates with distinct functional properties through integrated phenotypic and genomic evaluation, providing a basis for their further functional validation and application-oriented assessment.

title: Histological disappearance of persistent clarithromycin-resistant Helicobacter pylori infection following administration of a sulforaphane-, curcumin- and Lactobacillus-containing food supplement: a case report
abstract: Increasing antimicrobial resistance has become a major challenge in the treatment of Helicobacter pylori infection. Sulforaphane, a bioactive isothiocyanate derived from broccoli sprouts, has demonstrated anti-H. pylori activity in experimental and clinical studies. Curcumin and probiotic bacteria have also been investigated as adjunctive therapies. A woman in her seventies underwent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy screening. Histology revealed chronic active Helicobacter pylori-associated gastritis involving the antrum and corpus. Molecular testing confirmed H. pylori infection and detected the clarithromycin resistance mutation A2143G in the 23S rRNA gene. Following treatment with bismuth quadruple therapy consisting of Pylera® (Laboratoires Juvise Pharmaceuticals, France: bismuth subcitrate potassium 140 mg, metronidazole 125 mg and tetracycline hydrochloride 125 mg per capsule; three capsules four times daily) plus pantoprazole (40 mg twice daily for 10 days, followed by pantoprazole 40 mg once daily for 4 weeks), repeat endoscopy 1 year later demonstrated persistent active gastritis and persistence of the resistance mutation. The patient subsequently received a nutraceutical preparation containing broccoli-derived sulforaphane, curcumin, and Lactobacillus acidophilus. The preparation was administered as two capsules twice daily before meals for 21 days. Follow-up endoscopy approximately 3 months later demonstrated resolution of inflammatory activity and the absence of detectable H. pylori organisms in antral and corpus biopsies. This case documents the histological disappearance of persistent clarithromycin-resistant H. pylori infection following administration of a sulforaphane-, curcumin- and probiotic-containing nutraceutical. Although causality cannot be established from a single observation, the findings support further investigation of such interventions in patients with treatment-refractory infection.

title: Exosome based nanocarriers enabling effective treatment of antimicrobial resistant infections through improved delivery and clinical potential
abstract: Exosome-mediated drug delivery recently emerged as a viable approach for enhancing the therapeutic effectiveness of antimicrobial medicines in combating multidrug-resistant (MDR) pathogenic bacteria. Due to their inherent biocompatibility, biomimetic membrane structure, and effective cargo transport abilities, exosomes confront numerous drawbacks linked to traditional antimicrobial delivery systems, such as suboptimal drug stability, restricted biofilm infiltration, insufficient intracellular delivery, and unintended toxicity. This analysis offers an extensive summary of the latest developments in exosome-facilitated antimicrobial delivery, emphasising the conveyance of antibiotics, antimicrobial peptides, nucleic acids, and hybrid nanotherapeutics. Processes through which exosomes increase antimicrobial effectiveness, such as improved biofilm infiltration, intracellular localisation, immune system modulation, and precise cargo delivery, are comprehensively discussed. Recent advancements in exosome manipulation, cargo-loading methodologies, hybrid exosome-centric systems, and pathogen-specific delivery techniques are critically reviewed. Furthermore, this review discusses critical translational obstacles including scalable production, cargo-loading efficacy, quality assurance, storage durability, regulatory harmonisation, and clinical application. The evidence gathered highlights the potential of exosome-based delivery systems as novel biomimetic nanocarriers in the battle against antimicrobial resistance. It also highlights the technological and regulatory developments required for their successful clinical application.

title: AI-enhanced biosensing for antimicrobial resistance: translating rapid diagnostics to global surveillance
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) necessitates rapid and reliable diagnostic technologies to support timely antimicrobial selection and stewardship. Although conventional culture-based antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) remains clinically important, its extended turnaround time limits timely intervention, while molecular diagnostics can rapidly identify resistance determinants but may not accurately predict phenotypic resistance. This review critically examines the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) with biomedical microdevices and biosensors for rapid AMR detection, encompassing microfluidic and lab-on-chip platforms, electrochemical and optical biosensors, and CRISPR-based technologies. Emphasis is placed on the application of AI for signal processing, noise reduction, pattern recognition, multiplexed detection, and predictive interpretation of complex biosensor outputs. Key translational challenges, including biofouling, matrix interference, sample-preparation variability, bubble formation, evaporation, signal drift, invalid-test rates, device reproducibility, and inadequate standardisation of reporting and validation, are critically evaluated. The requirements for embedded AI, including memory, computational resources, latency, and energy efficiency, are also considered for portable point-of-care deployment. Analytical, clinical, and operational validation are distinguished, with emphasis on prospective multicentre evaluation using representative specimens and reference AST methods. Beyond clinical diagnosis, AI-enabled microdevices offer potential for decentralised AMR surveillance across wastewater, agricultural, veterinary, and environmental settings within a One Health framework. Translation will require standardised datasets, generalisable and explainable AI, scalable manufacturing, regulatory oversight, data governance, and equitable deployment. Overall, AI-integrated biomedical microdevices represent a promising approach to rapid, decentralised, and actionable AMR diagnostics and surveillance, contingent on robust real-world validation.

title: Whole-genome characterization of a food-derived Kurthia gibsonii isolate reveals a tet(L)-str-repUS12 resistance-associated region
abstract: The emergence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in environmental and food-associated bacteria has attracted increasing attention within the One Health framework. However, genomic information regarding antimicrobial resistance determinants and mobile genetic elements in Kurthia gibsonii remains limited. This study aimed to characterize a food-derived K. gibsonii isolate (KT09) by whole-genome sequencing, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and comparative genomic analysis, with emphasis on the genetic context of a tet(L)-associated resistance region. (KT09), recovered from phyllo dough on gentamicin-supplemented medium was sequenced using Illumina platform. The reported draft genome consisted of 2,944,613 bp in 122 contigs > 500 bp (GC content, 36.65%; N50, 72,389 bp), with 99.34% completeness and 2.87% contamination by CheckM. TYGS analysis confirmed assignment to K. gibsonii. Disk diffusion showed variable inhibition-zone diameters, with particularly small zones for tetracycline and streptomycin. Genome analysis identified tet(L), str, and aadA1, while emrB was detected by genome annotation. The tet(L)-str-repUS12 resistance-associated region was located on contig00014, which showed a mean read depth of 290.97× and 100% breadth of coverage. Comparative BLASTn and synteny analyses showed high nucleotide similarity between this localized region and homologous chromosomal and plasmid-associated sequences from Kurthia, Enterococcus, and Staphylococcus. However, the complete contig was predominantly Kurthia-like and was not resolved as an independent circular component. The KT09 genome expands the limited genomic information available for food-derived K. gibsonii and documents a tet(L)-str-repUS12 resistance-associated region with close sequence similarity to plasmid-associated loci reported in other Gram-positive bacteria. These findings are consistent with a shared mobile gene pool but do not establish plasmid localization, mobility, or the source or direction of horizontal gene transfer. Long-read sequencing and experimental plasmid characterization are required to resolve the genomic location and transferability of this region.

title: From Destruction to Reconstruction: Substrate-Driven Biosynthesis of Antioxidants from Antibiotic Residues in Hyperthermophilic Composting
abstract: The accumulation of tetracycline (TC) in organic fertilizers poses severe risks by fostering antibiotic resistance in soil ecosystems. Hyperthermophilic composting effectively mitigates these threats, achieving nearly complete TC removal via thermal selection. Although previous studies have widely characterized the catabolic degradation routes of TC, we propose a novel transformation pathway in which TC-derived intermediates are redirected into secondary metabolism to synthesize antioxidant alkaloids and flavonoids. Integrated abiotic-biotic controls first demonstrated that while heat initiates breakdown, hyperthermophilic microbiota drive the subsequent deep transformation and diversification of products. FT-ICR-MS revealed that this process is underpinned by substrate restructuring, where recalcitrant compounds are depolymerized into bioenergetically favorable low-molecular-weight organic matter (LMW-OM). Cross-feeding assays confirmed that this accessible substrate pool significantly enhances cometabolic efficiency compared to conventional composting-derived substrates. Mechanistically, multiomics indicated that LMW-OM elevates intracellular NADH and ATP within the Thermus-dominated community, shifting metabolism from maintenance to active biosynthesis. Consequently, TC intermediates acting as structural mimics of endogenous aromatic precursors are recruited into these energized pathways to generate antioxidants. Crucially, diverting residues into anabolic networks eliminates the selective pressure exerted by intermediates, explaining the extensive attenuation of the antibiotic resistance genes. This work highlights pivotal substrate-microbe interplay, offering a new paradigm for converting antibiotic-laden waste into functional bio-organic fertilizers.

title: Peptidoglycan remodeling prevents antibiotic resistance during oxidative stress
abstract: The bacterial small RNA (sRNA) OxyS is expressed induring oxidative stress. The sRNA OxyS enhances cell survival by controlling genes involved in the regulation of hydrogen peroxide (HO) and iron-sulfur (Fe-S) cluster formation. Here, we used the MS2 affinity purification coupled with RNA sequencing (MAPS) technique to identify new target mRNAs of the sRNA OxyS. Our analysis revealed a significant enrichment ofmRNA, which encodes a peptidoglycan endopeptidase that promotes cell growth. Our results confirm a previous report on the sRNA OxyS repressing the translation of. We also found that an Δbackground facilitates the emergence of mutations, conferring increased resistance to the last-resort antibiotics polymyxin B and E (colistin), but only in the presence of the targetgene. This suggests that the translation repression ofby OxyS could prevent mutations in bacterial DNA during HO-induced oxidative stress. Moreover, we show that adding the antioxidant thiourea or sequestering iron in the Δbackground effectively reduces the emergence of resistance against both polymyxin B and colistin. These results suggest that reactive oxygen species (ROS), in conjunction with intracellular iron, play a key role in driving the emergence of antibiotic resistance. Overall, our work underlines a mechanism of antimicrobial emergence implicating oxidative stress, intracellular Fe, and cell wall remodeling in.IMPORTANCEThis study uncovers an underexplored link between peptidoglycan remodeling and oxidative stress responses during exposure to antibiotics. By elucidating how MepS and the sRNA OxyS interact in the presence of polymyxins and oxidative stress, our study suggests that MepS may exert an anti-mutator function. The repression oftranslation by OxyS seems to limit the emergence of antibiotic resistance driven by DNA mutations. Together, these findings suggest cell wall remodeling and oxidative stress response pathways as promising targets to enhance antibiotic efficacy and limit the emergence of resistance.

title: Temporal Trends and Associations of Antimicrobial Use and Resistance in Enterococcus Species From Broiler Farms in Canada
authors: van den Bergh J et al.
abstract: Antimicrobials are widely used in animal production for the treatment, prevention, and control of infectious diseases. However, antimicrobial use (AMU) is also a key driver of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). In response, the Canadian poultry sector implemented a phased three-step AMU reduction strategy to mitigate the emergence and spread of AMR. Enterococci are ubiquitous inhabitants of the gastrointestinal tract of animals and serve as important sentinel organisms for AMR surveillance because of their capacity to acquire AMR. This study investigated associations between farm management practices, including AMU, and AMR in enterococci isolated from broiler chickens. Farm management data were collected using standardized questionnaires, and faecal samples were obtained during farm visits. Phenotypic AMR profiles were determined by minimum inhibitory concentration testing of 623 isolates from 419 flocks across five Canadian provinces over a 4-year period. Generalized linear mixed models were used to evaluate associations between AMR and other factors, including AMU, province, year, breed, stocking density, downtime between flocks, and sanitation practices. Avilamycin use was significantly associated with avilamycin resistance in both E. faecalis and E. faecium. Provincial and temporal differences in resistance were observed for certain antimicrobials, with a notable decline in resistant isolates to Veterinary Drugs Directorate's Category II and III antimicrobials following implementation of the three-step AMU reduction strategy. These findings suggest that targeted AMU reduction strategies were associated with reducing AMR percentages in enterococci from Canadian broilers.

title: Genomic rearrangement of the capsule operon in a phylogenetically distinct cluster of the multi-drug-resistant Escherichia coli lineage ST131
abstract: ST131 is a dominant cause of multi-drug-resistant extraintestinal infections in humans. The lineage has a three-clade phylogenetic structure, of which clade C has gained resistance to multiple classes of antibiotics and is globally disseminated. As well as antimicrobial resistance, a number of virulence factors contribute to the success of ST131 clade C, including the production of capsule. Previous work on a limited number of strains has shown that the capsule operon in ST131 is highly variable. In this study, we analyzed the capsule genetics ofST131 by interrogating 3,033 genomes. Our data show a clonal distribution of capsule types and identify a monophyletic group of ST131 clade C strains that are characterized by an atypical capsule operon with highly divergent alleles of the keyandgenes. Our analysis suggests there is ongoing evolution within clade C of ST131, which looks to be driven not by the continuing evolution of antimicrobial resistance but by host-pathogen interactions.IMPORTANCEMulti-drug-resistant (MDR)is a problematic cause of invasive disease in humans and animals. Resistance to multiple classes of antibiotics is severely limiting treatment options. ST131-C is a highly successful, MDR clone ofthat is a major cause of extraintestinal infections. Capsule is a key virulence factor in contributing to this clone's success, with capsule switching allowing the bacteria flexibility to thrive in different niches. We present evidence that suggests continual evolution of this proliferant clone influenced by host-pathogen interaction. Small genetic changes can define the success of a clone; therefore, it is important to monitor this continual evolution in pathogens.

title: Enterobacteriaceae and Bacteriophages: Implications Against Antimicrobial Resistance
abstract: Enterobacteriaceae represent a clinically challenging bacterial family owing to the global emergence of multidrug resistance. Bacteriophages, the natural predators of these bacteria, have emerged as powerful tools for detecting, targeting, and inhibiting these pathogens. This review provides a comprehensive overview of bacteriophages targeting Enterobacteriaceae hosts, focusing on their diversity, virion architecture, and the molecular determinants of host specificity. The dynamic co-evolution between bacterial defence strategies and phage counter-defences is discussed to illustrate the complexity of the phage-Enterobacteriaceae host interactions. Translational applications of Enterobacteriaceae phages, including phage therapy, engineered phages, phage-derived lysins as antimicrobials, and phage-based diagnostics for rapid and specific pathogen detection is also explored alongside their limitations including limited large-scale clinical trials, regulatory and manufacturing hurdles, and the need for robust host-range prediction and standardization. Overall, this review elaborates implications of bacteriophage-Enterobacteriaceae interactions to combat antimicrobial resistance and support the development of next-generation antibacterial therapies and diagnostics.

title: Understanding Host-Phage Interactions in Chronic Wounds, Emphasising Inflammatory Markers and Neutralising Antibody Responses
abstract: BackgroundChronic wounds cause considerable morbidity, which is further compounded by antimicrobial resistance and biofilm formation. Bacteriophage therapy (BT) presents a promising alternative. However, issues such as host immune neutralisation and inflammatory reactions remain unresolved.MethodsThis prospective, interventional, non-randomized control study was conducted at the Institute of Medical Sciences, Banaras Hindu University, from July 2022 to February 2026. It involved 100 patients with chronic wounds (>6 weeks). It had two groups: Group I (n = 50) received bacteriophage therapy (BT), while Group II (n = 50) received conventional therapy (CT). Bacteriophages were isolated and applied topically every other day. Serum levels of IL-1β, IL-6, MMP-9, and TGF-β were measured using ELISA at baseline, immediately after therapy, and at six weeks after treatment completion. Neutralising antibodies in the BT group were measured through serum-phage interaction assays and data analysis was done.ResultsFollow-up was completed in 90% of patients. Diabetes (50%) was the most common comorbidity. The most commonly isolated bacteria were(30%),(26%), and(26%). The therapy duration was significantly shorter ( < .001) in the BT group (1.46 ± 0.63 months) than in the CT group (2.92 ± 1.02 months). Levels of IL-1β, IL-6, MMP-9, and TGF-β decreased significantly in both groups during and after treatment. Neutralising antibodies were detected in only 2 out of 45 BT patients (4.4%) with complete follow-up.ConclusionBT promoted faster wound healing without notably altering cytokine profiles. The fact that around 4.4% of patients developed neutralising antibodies, which did not interfere with healing, suggests that phage therapy can be safely applied.

title: Are Higher-Order Carbapenems Effective Therapy for Patients with Ertapenem-Resistant Enterobacterales Invasive Infections?
abstract: The IDSA guidance suggests treating Enterobacterales resistant to ertapenem but susceptible to imipenem or meropenem with a susceptible carbapenem in the absence of carbapenemase production; however, clinical outcomes data are limited. We conducted a multicenter prospective cohort study of hospitalized patients with invasive ceftriaxone-resistant Enterobacterales infections, comparing 30-day mortality between ertapenem-susceptible (ETP-S) and ertapenem-resistant (ETP-R) isolates. ETP-S isolates with an ESBL/AmpC phenotype served as the comparator because carbapenems are reliably active against these organisms. Carbapenem susceptibility was confirmed by broth microdilution. Inclusion criteria included: (1) susceptibility to imipenem or meropenem, (2) absence of carbapenemase genes, and (3) >72 hours of definitive therapy with imipenem or meropenem. Inverse probability weighting (IPW) adjusted for baseline differences, and logistic regression estimated odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals. Among 374 patients, 238 (64%) were infected with ETP-S and 136 (36%) ETP-R isolates. Baseline characteristics were balanced after IPW. ETP-R infection was associated with higher 30-day mortality (OR 2.24, 95% CI 1.26-3.98, p=0.006). Similarly, 14-day and in-hospital mortality were significantly higher among patients with ETP-R infections. The highest mortality was observed among patients with isolates resistant to two carbapenems (e.g., ertapenem and meropenem). Genomic analyses demonstrated enrichment of porin alterations and more non-carbapenemase β-lactamase genes (e.g., blaCTX-M, blaOXA-10) in ETP-R isolates. Among patients with Enterobacterales bacteremia treated with imipenem or meropenem, ETP-R isolates were associated with higher mortality than ETP-S isolates, challenging current guidance. This likely reflects combined porin loss and increased β-lactamase activity, potentially resulting in partial hydrolysis of higher-order carbapenems despite in vitro susceptibility.

title: Predictors of Antibiotic Overuse in Febrile Children: A Sub-analysis of the Prospective, Multicenter AutoPilot-Dx Study
abstract: Antibiotic overuse contributes to antimicrobial resistance. Mechanisms that drive overuse, including diagnostic uncertainty, are thought to be complex. We aimed to investigate predictive factors for antibiotic overuse in a large pediatric cohort. This is a subanalysis from the AutoPilot-Dx study, which enrolled febrile children 90 days to 18 years old presenting to the pediatric emergency department with respiratory tract infection or fever without source, including both hospitalized children and those discharged home. We analyzed patient flow from being treated with antibiotics at recruitment to definitive antibiotic treatment after assessment, depending on physician judgment. Variables significantly associated with antibiotic overuse in univariate analysis were entered into a multivariable logistic regression model to identify independent predictors of antibiotic overuse, defined as receipt of antibiotic treatment following clinical assessment in cases with viral panel-adjudicated diagnosis. Diagnostic uncertainty was assessed by treating physicians. Upon recruitment, 127/1008 (12.6%) were receiving antibiotic treatment. Overall, 186 of 628 cases with a viral panel-adjudicated diagnosis were judged to have antibiotic overuse. Factors with significant association in univariate analysis were diagnostic uncertainty, nonexudative tonsillitis, rales and younger age. Presence of a diagnostic test result upon presentation to the hospital and current antibiotic treatment were found not to be associated with overuse. Among 566 of 1008 cases with complete data on all model covariates, multivariable logistic regression yielded diagnostic uncertainty [odds ratio (OR), 2.09; 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.18-3.93; P = 0.015], nonexudative tonsillitis (OR, 2.78; 95% CI: 1.72-4.59; P < 0.001) and rales (OR, 1.82; 95% CI: 1.15-2.86; P = 0.01) to be positively associated with antibiotic overuse, while age showed a negative association in complete-case analysis (OR, 0.93; 95% CI: 0.85-0.99; P = 0.038), which attenuated and was no longer significant in a multiple imputation sensitivity analysis (OR, 0.96; 95% CI: 0.91-1.01; P = 0.150). Diagnostic uncertainty contributes to antibiotic overuse, alongside clinical factors. Future studies should investigate the impact of improved diagnostic algorithms on antibiotic prescribing in patients with respiratory tract infections in whom physicians experience diagnostic uncertainty.

title: The role, challenges, and innovations of rifampin in the management of periprosthetic joint infections: a narrative review
abstract: Periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) remains a severe complication due to persistent bacterial biofilms. Rifampin is traditionally valued for its unique biofilm-penetrating properties, yet its clinical role is increasingly viewed as context-dependent. While current evidence supports the efficacy of rifampin in two-stage revision arthroplasty, its application in debridement, antibiotics, and implant retention (DAIR) remains a subject of ongoing debate. Landmark randomized trials once reported superior cure rates for DAIR combined with rifampin, but contemporary large-scale retrospective data show no statistically significant difference in remission rates, often accompanied by a significantly higher incidence of adverse events. Furthermore, the timing of administration is critical; early initiation within five days post-DAIR has been linked to increased treatment failure. These challenges, alongside profound drug-drug interactions, have spurred interest in localized delivery innovations like microencapsulation and nanoparticles. While these bioengineering approaches show preclinical promise in overcoming PMMA chemical incompatibility, they remain at the proof-of-concept stage. Consequently, rifampin should be employed as a targeted adjunct rather than a universal standard, requiring careful consideration of surgical strategy, patient tolerance, and optimal timing.

title: Carbonaceous nanomaterials for the removal of hazardous pharmaceutical contaminants from wastewater: mechanisms, recent advances, and future directions
abstract: Rising pharmaceutical consumption and the continuous discharge of pharmaceutically active compounds (PhACs) into aquatic systems have become defining environmental challenges of the present decade. Because conventional wastewater treatment plants were never designed to remove biologically persistent micropollutants, trace residues accumulate in surface water, groundwater and drinking water, where they drive ecotoxicity, endocrine disruption and the dissemination of antibiotic-resistance genes. Therefore, understanding how nanomaterials can not only capture but also destroy these contaminants is central to safeguarding water quality. This review critically examines carbonaceous nanomaterials, such as graphene oxide, reduced graphene oxide, carbon nanotubes, graphitic carbon nitride, carbon dots and biochar, for PhAC removal, organised around the four dominant treatment routes: adsorption, membrane filtration, advanced oxidation processes (AOPs) and photocatalysis, the latter treated here as a light-driven hazard-oriented framework that achieves true mineralisation rather than the mere transfer of contaminants to another phase. The best-performing systems for the removal of representative drug classes, such as antibiotics, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, antidepressants, β-blockers and analgesics, are shown to share a common design motif: a conductive, defect-rich and often heteroatom-doped carbon scaffold that concentrates the pollutant, shuttles photogenerated charge carriers and stabilises a redox or light-active phase. Adsorption and membrane filtration routes deliver high capacity but relocate contaminants to a solid or concentrated phase, while carbon-coupled AOPs and S-/Z-scheme heterojunctions achieve contaminant degradation with concurrent antibiotic-resistance-gene reduction.
